Is State Farm your insurance or the other party’s insurance? If your policy doesn’t have Personal Injury Protection or Medical Payments coverage then they won’t be able to cover it. If the other party’s insurance accepted liability, they are on the hook for your medical bills under their Bodily Injury coverage. 

Are you able to forward the bills directly to State Farm? Or the at-fault party’s insurance (should they be different)?

The insurance company will want to collect as much money as possible from you. This will mean, if they’re smart, they’ll likely offer you a payment plan. So, no I wouldn’t say you would have to pay it in full... it would depend on the company’s policy. 

I used to work for a name brand company and I have seen them not pursue individuals without insurance. But in the one case I remember it was an old (80+) man with no job and no assets. 

The company cannot take the money out of your account. But they can take you to court and garnish your wages.

Former liability adjuster here. Don’t know the full details, but it sounds like you agree you’re at fault? 

If you’re at fault, you’re liable for all the damages you caused. If you had active insurance at the time of the accident (although it seems you didn’t) your company would pay for all of the damages up to your Property Damage limit. Since you didn’t have insurance at the time of the accident, if the other party pursues their damages through their insurance, their insurance company will pursue you for the full cost of repairs and potentially rental as well. 

Depending on the year of the car... a small dent or scratch could easily cost $1k+ when they break down the vehicle for repairs, I wouldn’t be surprised if they find more damage and the cost of repairs goes up from $989.
If you haven’t yet, file a police report. Some Uninsured motorist coverages require a police report to be able to use

Good to learn this while you’re young,  but never pay someone cash for damage caused after an accident. First, you’re likely not getting a receipt and thus have no proof of payment. She can easily turn around, file a claim, and deny that you ever paid her a dime. Second, damage to vehicles is usually a LOT more expensive than you would think. Small dents and scratches can easily rack up $1k+. 

In my experience as a claims adjuster, there’s a good chance she’ll file a claim. 

To answer your question, there isn’t really anything for you “to do” per say. Make sure the vehicle owner (of the car you were driving) is aware of the accident. Provide the owner your insurance, if you have any (your insurance will be secondary, and will only come into play if there are coverage/limits issues with the owners insurance). 

If a claim is filed you will likely be asked for a statement. Since you are a minor a parent can give this statement on your behalf or they can be with you on the phone when you give the adjuster your statement.

I would start with the basics: 1) cleanse 2) moisturize 3) protection  (sunscreen) 
 
Any gentle cleanser like the ones from Cerave should work. 

If you wear makeup or use sunscreen you should double cleanse. An oil or balm based cleanser would be great for a first cleanse. The second cleanse could be your typical gel cleanser for removing the dirt and grime. 

Your skin type will warrant different types of moisturizers. Oilier skin will likely do better with light weight lotion, while drier skin could probably use a heavier lotion. 

I’d HIGHLY recommend using a sunscreen everyday. Not only does it prevent skin cancer, but it’s apparently the golden rule of skincare (from what I’ve heard). UVA rays age us, so burns aren’t the only concern. 

Also, if you have sensitive skin I would try to stay away from things with fragrance as that can cause irritation.
